why: A refresh that faults must end the inner sequence, not the outer subscription. Rethrowing kills the deferred-refresh stream permanently, so the list silently stops updating.
The whole point of the prefix clause. A revert costs the index and re-sorts the library, but produces a byte-identical query plan - only a structural assertion catches it.
find: substr(c.content, 1, 64) ASC, c.content COLLATE BINARY ASC

why: The clause prefix and the index expression must agree. Changing one and not the other silently drops back to a full sort.
substr() returns a BINARY result and does not inherit the column collation, but bare c.content does. A NOCASE column leaves the two halves of the ORDER BY disagreeing.
Every sort needs its own pinned-prefixed index. Without one, the sort falls back to a temp B-tree over the whole library (252ms at 20k clips).
Same, for the expression index. Partial index coverage measured worse than none at all.
Disabling a sensitivity rule stops having any effect. Found by audit: this survived all 278 non-headless tests before SensitivityServiceTests existed.
Scan runs on the capture path against user-authored regexes. Unbounded backtracking hangs clipboard capture: "(a+)+$" over 32 chars had not returned after three minutes.
Compiling leniently on save lets an invalid pattern reach the database, which is the original bug: it was stored, then threw, and every later load threw on it too.
Strict compilation on load makes one bad stored pattern take down the entire rule set, leaving sensitivity scanning permanently unable to load.
